**Find the first nonfinite value rather than guessing a fix.** A NaN loss can originate in the data, forward computation, loss, backward pass, or optimizer state. The later it appears in the log, the less obvious the original cause becomes. Preserve the failing batch and seed so the failure is reproducible. [1](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/index.html)

First verify finite inputs/targets, valid labels, and sensible scales. Run a tiny forward pass in FP32 and inspect intermediate ranges. Check custom divisions, square roots, exponentials, and logarithms; `log(0)`, invalid square roots, and all-masked softmax rows are common causes.

Next inspect gradients before the optimizer step. If forward/loss are finite but gradients are not, use anomaly detection or targeted hooks around the first failing operation. Then inspect parameter and optimizer-state values after the update. A very large learning rate can turn a finite gradient into an unstable parameter jump.

Compare with a trusted loss or layer and disable mixed precision temporarily. If FP32 succeeds while FP16 fails, investigate overflow/underflow and scaling rather than masking the NaN with zeros. Reduce the problem until one batch can train reliably.

Change one cause at a time and rerun the saved failure. Gradient clipping or a lower rate may help a genuine scale problem, but neither repairs shuffled labels, invalid arithmetic, or corrupted input. Record the root cause and add a regression check for that failure instead of treating “training no longer crashes” as complete validation.

**Technical details and references.**

First reproduce on one fixed batch in FP32 and locate the **first** nonfinite tensor, rather than inspecting only the final loss. Check input/target ranges and label validity; then intermediate activations, the custom loss, gradients, and optimizer state. [1](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/index.html) [2](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/amp_examples.html)

Use stable primitives such as log-softmax/BCE-with-logits; avoid evaluating invalid operations before masking them. Verify learning rate, initialization, reduction denominators, normalization, and gradient clipping after unscaling. If FP32 works but FP16 fails, inspect overflow and scaler behavior. If both fail at the same operation, precision is probably not the root cause.

After the first bad operation is understood, fix it and rerun the minimal batch before returning to distributed training. Save the triggering data and state as a regression case; blindly reducing learning rate can hide a genuine formula or data error.
